title: Neon Driftline Classic: releasing an AI-assisted Godot arcade game (free web / $1 Android)
author: dcdisco
selftext:
Commercial self-promotion + AI disclosure: this is my DMC Oddworks game, made with AI-assisted code in Godot. The neon shapes and sound effects are generated procedurally in the game.



Neon Driftline Classic is a small space survival arcade game: dodge, dash, earn upgrades and try again. You start with two hits and no weapon. Research carries between runs on the same device.



The interesting part of getting it ready for release was checking what the AI-assisted build actually did. A successful export was not enough. A percent-formatting bug needed a real fix, smoke tests needed fresh save data so old progress did not hide problems, and the paid Android edition needed its ad SDK/bridge removed rather than just hiding an ad button. The final APK requests no Android permissions.



For the web build, shrinking the canvas with CSS stretched the game. Putting the unchanged export inside an iframe below a persistent ad strip preserved the aspect ratio and input area. The free edition keeps that advertising space visible; the $1 Android download is ad-free and works offline.



Play free: [https://sites.google.com/view/neon-driftline-classic](https://sites.google.com/view/neon-driftline-classic)

Android APK ($1, direct download rather than Google Play): [https://payhip.com/b/qGWZf](https://payhip.com/b/qGWZf)



For people shipping AI-assisted games: what is the first test you run to catch a release that exports fine but does not actually play correctly? I would also like feedback on the opening difficulty—two hits and no starting weapon is deliberate, but it needs to feel fair.
